new_statements.quote: This article investigates whether lexical frequency drives stress assignment in Greek, a morphology-dependent stress system. [...] Adults show systematic inflection-class conditioning: their stress patterns broadly follow the lexicon's dominant stress pattern per inflection class but depart from its distributional frequencies. Children exhibit a strong, frequency-insensitive preference for penultimate stress that persists across inflection classes, with only traces of suffix-specific stress preferences emerging in Grade 6. We argue that lexical frequency operates within grammatically imposed boundaries: the phonological default and inflection-class conditioning together determine the extent to which distributional patterns in the lexicon shape stress assignment.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Greek word stress is not phonologically predictable: it is a 'morphology-dependent' system in which the stress of a noun is conditioned by its inflection class (adults follow each class's dominant pattern) on top of a phonological default; children, before they have learned the class conditioning, put stress on the penult by default. The abstract does not state which syllable the adult phonological default is.
new_statements.exceptions: Children in Grades 3 and 6 show a frequency-insensitive penultimate preference across inflection classes; adults depart from lexical frequency distributions while following the dominant pattern per class.

new_statements.quote: Greek is a morphology-dependent stress system, where stress is lexically specified for a number of individual morphemes (e.g., roots and suffixes). In the absence of lexically encoded stress, a default stress emerges. Most theoretical analyses of Greek stress that assume antepenultimate stress to represent the default (e.g., Malikouti-Drachman & Drachman 1989; Ralli & Touratzidis 1992; Revithiadou 1999) are not independently confirmed by experimental studies [...] two production (reading aloud) experiments, which revealed, for our consultants, first, an almost complete lack of antepenultimate stress and, second, a split between penultimate and final stress dependent on acronym length, the type of the final segment and the syllable type of the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexically specified on individual morphemes (roots, suffixes), so it is not predictable from phonology; a default emerges only where no morpheme carries lexical stress. The theoretical antepenultimate default is not experimentally confirmed: in acronyms (no overt morphology) speakers almost never use antepenultimate stress, splitting instead between penultimate and final stress according to length, final segment (consonant-final acronyms take final stress) and penult syllable type; vowel-final acronyms tend to copy the stress of the inflected word they stand for; otherwise speakers prefer stress at stem edges.
new_statements.exceptions: Acronyms: consonant-final ones take end stress; vowel-final ones follow the inflected word they represent when enough morphonological information is available; antepenultimate stress is almost absent in acronyms.
new_statements.identity_note: All works concern Standard Modern Greek; none describes a particular dialect. Papangeli 2004 (indexes 5 and 6) is one dissertation listed twice by Glottolog (Dutch and English title forms).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with and adds detail to the existing enclisis note (van Oostendorp 2012: enclisis adds a second stress on the last two syllables); here the added stress is explicitly transcribed as secondary and comes from Janse 1997. The thesis as a whole describes Ancient Greek (metrics, caesura, crasis, aphaeresis, Wackernagel clitics), where it treats accent only as the property that distinguishes tonic from atonic (clitic) pronoun series (p. 195: 'los pronombres personales de 1a y 2a persona en griego contrastan en el singular una serie tónica y una serie átona'); it has no section on the nature or placement of the Greek accent.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule for Modern Greek word stress is given. The one Modern Greek stress statement is that an enclitic possessive attached to a word with antepenultimate stress adds a secondary stress on the host's final syllable (δάσκαλός μου [ˈðas.ka.ˌloz.mu]), with the primary stress staying on the antepenult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Enclisis-induced secondary stress on the host's last syllable, transcribed with a secondary-stress mark ([ˈðas.ka.ˌloz.mu]).
new_statements.identity_note: Three of the seven listed works describe Ancient Greek, not Modern Greek (mode1248): Goodwin 1897 (Classical Greek verb syntax), Bopp 1854 (comparative grammar; Ancient Greek, although the MPG PuRe record tags ISO 639-3 ell) and Pardal Padín 2017 (Ancient Greek metrics and clitics, with one Modern Greek footnote). Angelopoulos & Sportiche 2018 concerns Standard Modern Greek; Philippaki-Warburton 1998, Nespor & Ralli 1996 and Reed & Bartolotta 2014 are Modern Greek but could not be opened.

readall_conflicts: On the type of system there is no disagreement: the two abstracts I could read (Revithiadou, Nikolou & Papadopoulou 2015; Revithiadou et al. 2026) both call Greek a morphology-dependent stress system in which stress is lexically specified on morphemes, which is the catalog's lexical coding and van Oostendorp's (2012) statement. They disagree with the existing statement on the default: van Oostendorp says antepenultimate stress is the default, whereas the 2015 abstract states that the antepenultimate default assumed by Malikouti-Drachman & Drachman 1989, Ralli & Touratzidis 1992 and Revithiadou 1999 'is not independently confirmed by experimental studies' and that acronyms show 'an almost complete lack of antepenultimate stress', splitting between penultimate and final stress; the 2026 abstract adds that children default to penultimate stress across inflection classes. Neither abstract states the adult phonological default syllable, so the default remains contested rather than settled; the acronym result is domain-specific (morphology-free words) and the child result is developmental.

sources.quote: Die Tonverschiebung vollzieht sich im Alt- und Neugriechischen tatsächlich nach dem gleichen Gesetz: das ursprüngliche Wort wird auf der letzten, das abgeleitete auf der vorletzten Silbe betont. Und wie im Altgriechischen, so ist auch im Neugriechischen mit dieser Verschiebung des Tons nicht nur eine solche der Bedeutung, sondern sogar eine solche der Funktion verbunden. [The accent shift proceeds in Ancient and Modern Greek by the same law: the base word is stressed on the final, the derived word on the penultimate syllable; and in Modern Greek as in Ancient Greek this shift of accent is tied not only to a shift of meaning but even of function.]
sources.note: Historical-derivational study: accent retraction (oxytone base > paroxytone derivative, e.g. kontós 'short' > Kóntos name; adverbs from prepositions) is a productive lexical/morphological device in Medieval and Modern Greek, so accent position is contrastive and word-specific. Consistent with the 'lexical' coding; silent on the three-syllable window and default.
